lines.text: The microwave oven exists because a candy bar melted in an engineer's pocket.
And that's not even the strangest one. Before this video ends, you'll know how two scientists blamed pigeons, and found the beginning of the universe.
Some of the most important things ever made were mistakes. Wrong parts. Dirty hands. Spoiled fruit. Today, ten accidents that changed the world, and the strange stories behind them.
Every story is real, and checked. Sources are in the description. Let's go.
Number one.
In nineteen fifty-seven, two inventors sealed two sheets of plastic together, and trapped rows of air bubbles inside.
lines.caption: In 1957, two inventors sealed two sheets of plastic together, and trapped rows of air bubbles inside.

lines.text: Their big idea? A modern, textured wallpaper.
It turns out, nobody wanted bubbles on their walls. The wallpaper flopped.
So they hunted for another use, and found one: wrapping fragile things for shipping.
The wallpaper that failed now protects packages all over the world. And it's fun to pop.
Number two.
In nineteen sixty-eight, a chemist made an adhesive that was, well, weak. It stuck, but it peeled right off, and left nothing behind.
lines.caption: In 1968, a chemist made an adhesive that was, well, weak. It stuck, but it peeled right off, and left nothing behind.

lines.text: For years, nobody could figure out what it was good for.
Then a colleague who sang in a church choir had an annoying problem. His paper bookmarks kept falling out of his hymn book.
So he coated them with the weak glue. They stayed put, and peeled off without tearing a single page.
In nineteen eighty, sticky notes went on sale across America. Today they're in offices everywhere.
lines.caption: In 1980, sticky notes went on sale across America. Today they're in offices everywhere.

lines.text: Number three.
In the late eighteen seventies, a chemist was working with substances made from coal tar.
lines.caption: In the late 1870s, a chemist was working with substances made from coal tar.

lines.text: Then he sat down to dinner, and noticed something odd. His bread tasted strangely sweet.
The sweetness wasn't in the bread. It was on him. He'd carried it home from the lab.
He traced it back to a chemical he'd been working on. It was about three hundred times sweeter than sugar.
lines.caption: He traced it back to a chemical he'd been working on. It was about 300 times sweeter than sugar.

lines.text: That chemical is saccharin, one of the oldest artificial sweeteners. Found by tasting dinner.
Chemists have a golden rule: never taste your work. He broke it by accident, at the dinner table.
lines.caption: Chemists have a golden rule: never taste your work. He broke it by accident, at the dinner table.

lines.text: Number four.
In nineteen forty-two, during World War Two, researchers were trying to make crystal-clear plastic for gun sights.
lines.caption: In 1942, during World War Two, researchers were trying to make crystal-clear plastic for gun sights.

lines.text: One family of chemicals had a big problem. It stuck to everything it touched.
Useless. So it was rejected.
Nine years later, the same chemist ran into it again, while working on canopies for jet planes. This time, he saw what it really was: an incredibly strong glue.
lines.caption: Nine years later, the same chemist ran into it again, while working on canopies for jet planes. This time, he saw what it really was: an incredibly strong glue.

lines.text: It went on sale in nineteen fifty-eight. And during the Vietnam War, medics reportedly sprayed it on wounds to stop bleeding.
lines.caption: It went on sale in 1958. And during the Vietnam War, medics reportedly sprayed it on wounds to stop bleeding.

lines.text: Number five.
Back to that candy bar. Around the end of World War Two, an engineer was working next to a magnetron, the device that powered radar.
He noticed the candy bar in his pocket had melted. He hadn't felt a thing.
Curious, he held popcorn kernels near it. They popped.
The first microwave oven went on sale a couple of years later. It stood nearly six feet tall, and weighed about seven hundred and fifty pounds.
lines.caption: The first microwave oven went on sale a couple of years later. It stood nearly 6 feet tall, and weighed about 750 pounds.

lines.text: That's about as heavy as five adults. And the inventor? He had left school when he was about twelve.
lines.caption: That's about as heavy as 5 adults. And the inventor? He had left school when he was about 12.

lines.text: Number six.
In nineteen thirty-eight, a young chemist was experimenting with a gas for refrigerators.
lines.caption: In 1938, a young chemist was experimenting with a gas for refrigerators.

lines.text: One day, he opened the valve on a cylinder of it. Nothing came out.
Empty? But on the scale, it weighed just as much as before.
So they cut the cylinder open. Inside was a white, waxy, super slippery powder. The gas had turned into a solid, all by itself.
That powder became the non-stick coating on frying pans.
But its first big job was top secret: sealing valves in the Manhattan Project, the wartime program that built the first atomic bomb.
Number seven.
In nineteen fifty-six, an engineer was building a circuit to record the sounds of the heart.
lines.caption: In 1956, an engineer was building a circuit to record the sounds of the heart.

lines.text: He reached into a box, grabbed a resistor, and plugged it in. It was the wrong one.
When he switched it on, the circuit didn't record anything. It pulsed. Steady. Like a heartbeat.
He realized this could keep the beat for a heart that had lost its rhythm. So he shrank it down to fit inside a person.
Within a few years, it was keeping real patients alive. Since then, pacemakers have helped millions of people.
Think about that. One mix-up with a tiny part became a machine that keeps human hearts beating.
Number eight.

scene.title: THE GLOW IN THE DARK LAB

lines.text: In November eighteen ninety-five, a physicist in Germany was experimenting with a glass tube that fired invisible rays.
lines.caption: In November 1895, a physicist in Germany was experimenting with a glass tube that fired invisible rays.

lines.text: Then he noticed something that shouldn't happen. A coated screen nearby was glowing.
Some unknown ray was passing straight through things. Paper. Wood. Even skin.
One of his first X-ray pictures showed his wife's hand. Her bones, and her wedding ring.
Within weeks, the news had spread around the world.
And then it got weird. From the nineteen twenties to the fifties, thousands of shoe stores had X-ray machines, so customers could see the bones of their feet inside new shoes.
lines.caption: And then it got weird. From the 1920s to the '50s, thousands of shoe stores had X-ray machines, so customers could see the bones of their feet inside new shoes.

lines.text: We now know that wasn't safe, and states began banning them.
Number nine.
In nineteen twenty-eight, a scientist came back from a holiday to a messy lab, with old dishes of bacteria still lying around.
lines.caption: In 1928, a scientist came back from a holiday to a messy lab, with old dishes of bacteria still lying around.

lines.text: One dish of bacteria had been invaded by mold. And all around the mold, the bacteria were dead.
That mold was making penicillin, the world's first antibiotic.
But making it was brutally hard. In early nineteen forty-two, there was only enough to treat a single patient.

lines.text: Then, in Peoria, Illinois, someone brought a moldy cantaloupe from the market into the lab.
The mold on that melon made far more penicillin than Fleming's original. Production took off.
A rotten melon helped turn a miracle drug into an everyday medicine.
And number ten. The one I promised.

scene.title: THE PIGEON PROBLEM
scene.sub: The echo of the Big Bang

lines.text: In nineteen sixty-four, two radio astronomers in New Jersey had a giant horn-shaped antenna, and a very annoying problem.
lines.caption: In 1964, two radio astronomers in New Jersey had a giant horn-shaped antenna, and a very annoying problem.

lines.text: A faint hiss. It came from every direction in the sky, day and night, season after season. They thought their equipment was broken.
Then they found the suspects. Pigeons, nesting inside the antenna. And their droppings.
So they evicted the pigeons and scrubbed the antenna clean.
The hiss was still there.
Because it wasn't coming from the antenna. It was coming from the universe itself. The faint afterglow of the Big Bang, some of the earliest light ever released.
Their annoying noise was evidence of how the universe began. It won them the Nobel Prize in Physics in nineteen seventy-eight.
lines.caption: Their annoying noise was evidence of how the universe began. It won them the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1978.

lines.text: And here's the wildest part. If you've ever seen the fuzzy static on an old TV between channels, a small fraction of that fuzz was the same afterglow. You were watching the Big Bang.
Quick recap. Bubble wrap was failed wallpaper. Sticky notes came from a weak glue. Saccharin was found on a chemist's hands.
Super glue was too sticky. A candy bar melted. A tank wasn't empty. A resistor was wrong.
A screen glowed. A melon got moldy. And pigeons led to the Big Bang.
